title: Home in ordinary clothes
hookLine: back at Kartarpur, Nanak lays down the pilgrim's robe and lives as a householder (Bhai Gurdas, Var 1)

cards: The suitcase goes down in the hall. The shoes come off. The clothes that smell of trains and other people's cities go into the wash, and you pull on the soft old things you only wear at home.
There's a particular relief in that moment: the trip is over, and ordinary life can start again. Bhai Gurdas gives Guru Nanak that moment too, after the mountain, Mecca and Baghdad. Today: udasi.

teach.b: Bhai Gurdas says: then Baba came to Kartarpur, and took off the whole garb of the udasi, the wandering renunciant.

teach.h: A HOUSEHOLDER, ON A SIMPLE COT.
teach.b: He put on the clothes of a householder, worldly clothes, and sat on a manji, a simple cot, and taught from there. Year one told you about the farmer at Kartarpur, working the land by the river. Today, look at the clothes.
On the road, Nanak wore the wanderer's garb. At home, he takes it off, and nothing about him says holy man to a passerby. He looks like anyone in the village.
Bhai Gurdas doesn't treat this as a step down. He tells it as the point.

teach.h: THE HOLINESS WASN'T IN THE ROBE.
teach.b: The holiness didn't live in the robe, so taking the robe off costs nothing. Then he tells what daily life at Kartarpur sounded like. The Guru's word was spoken there, he says, and light spread and darkness went.

teach.h: JAPJI AT DAWN, SODAR AT EVENING.
teach.b: Sodar and Aarti, the evening hymns, were sung, and the Japji was recited at amritvela, the early hours before dawn.
That's the shape of the day you learned all last year: the Japji before sunrise, the evening prayers at dusk.

In Bhai Gurdas's telling, it's already there at Kartarpur, kept by a man in ordinary clothes, in an ordinary village, between the farming and the meals. Holiness came home, and it looked like a routine.

how: Sikhs live as householders rather than renunciants, working, raising families and keeping the daily banis at home, and they point to Guru Nanak's life at Kartarpur as the pattern.

games.q: you're coming home after years on the road as a well-known holy traveler. what do you wear now?
o: the traveler's robe, so people know who you are.
ordinary clothes, like everyone in the village.
something grander, for a teacher with followers.
games.why: Bhai Gurdas says Nanak took off the whole garb of the udasi and put on worldly clothes. the holiness wasn't in the robe.

practice: Choose one small task right in front of you, washing a cup, folding a shirt, watering a plant, and do it slowly, with your full attention, as if it were the most important thing in the house, because for these few minutes it is.
No special clothes, no special place; if you pray, you can let Waheguru ride along with each movement.

wordCard.voice: Udasi, the wandering renunciant's garb Nanak set aside at Kartarpur, taking up a householder's clothes and keeping the daily prayers there.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: a wandering renunciant. Bhai Gurdas says Nanak took off the udasi's garb at Kartarpur.

carryVoice: Your line: holy in ordinary clothes. The robe came off, and nothing holy went with it. That's day seven hundred four.

sources.ref: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Var 1, pauri 38 (Kartarpur: the udasi's garb set aside; Sodar, Aarti and the Japji)
